To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
phylogenetically related species are more likely to be similar in traits related to cadmium bioaccumulation and that these differences among species may be predicted based on phylogeny.
phylogenetically based approaches to ecophysiological studies can reveal patterns of diversity that would not otherwise be apparent.

phylogenetically based analyses of ecophysiological traits related to cadmium susceptibility reveal that: (1) species are generally similar to their close relatives in these traits; (2) the strength of phylogenetic signal in these traits varies among traits; (3) phylogeny is a more important predictor of physiological performance than functional traits; and (4) there appears to be a tradeoff between Cd elimination and detoxification in mayflies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of ecophysiological traits in aquatic insect taxa, and how these traits may be used to predict species responses to environmental stress, in this case the trace metal Cd.
the effects of environmental stressors on aquatic insects, and the use of phylogenetic information to understand these responses.
the evolution of insect susceptibility to environmental stressors, specifically cadmium, a common pollutant in aquatic ecosystems
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

phylogenetically based studies of ecophysiological traits are an effective way to identify and quantify differences in susceptibility to stressors among species and to identify potential tradeoffs between physiological traits.
the phylogeny-based comparative method has been used successfully to identify patterns and predict variation in ecophysiological traits related to cadmium susceptibility in aquatic insects.

the use of a phylogenetic comparative approach can reveal the presence of evolutionary patterns in traits related to Cd susceptibility and that these patterns are important for understanding the variation in Cd bioaccumulation potential across insect species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phylogenetic information should be used in the design of experiments and interpretation of results, especially when comparing species from different taxonomic groups.
phylogenetic comparative analyses can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying interspecific variation in ecophysiological traits.
phylogenetic comparative approaches can reveal important information about the physiological basis for differences in species susceptibility to environmental stressors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

phylogenetically based analyses are essential for understanding the physiological basis of variation in susceptibility to stressors among species, and that the use of such analyses will be critical for understanding the ecological and evolutionary impacts of stressors in nature.

phylogenetically informed physiological approaches are likely to reveal patterns of trait variation that can be used to better predict the responses of species to environmental stressors, and to better predict the effects of environmental stressors on species.

phylogenetically based analyses can reveal the importance of evolutionary processes in the generation of diversity in ecophysiological traits, and can be used to predict the physiological performance of taxa based on their phylogenetic position.
